newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Defector talks stall, Seoul says North near crisis.
newsitem.headline: Defector talks stall, Seoul says North near crisis.

text.p: South Korea said on Wednesday talks were stalled on the fate of a senior North Korean defector in Seoul's Beijing embassy, and the head of the South's ruling party said Pyongyang was nearing a final crisis.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman denied a Japanese newspaper report that China and South Korea had agreed that Hwang Jang-yop, ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy, could leave Beijing for asylum in South Korea as early as this week.
North Korea had earlier indicated it was softening its stance over Hwang, a top ideologue whose defection marks one of the greatest embarrassments for the Stalinist state.
"Unfortunately, we have not made any real progress in our talks with China and it is too early to talk about when Hwang could leave Beijing," spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung told Reuters.
Another Foreign Ministry official, who asked not to be identified, said: "He is not likely to leave within a few days. It could be weeks before Hwang can secure his departure."
Japan's Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that Seoul and Beijing had "basically agreed to transfer Hwang" to South Korea.
Hwang has taken refuge at the heavily-guarded South Korean consular office in Beijing for eight days.

Highlighting concern in South Korea that the defection showed serious instability in Pyongyang, Lee Hong-koo of the ruling New Korea Party warned that Seoul must re-think its unification policy towards the North.

"Severe food shortages and economic difficulties are driving the North Korean system to an irreversible final crisis," Lee told parliament. "In view of North Korea's rapid breaking away from its orbit and its plunge, we must drastically review our unification policy."

Lee, who said Hwang's defection was pushing the North's leadership into desperation, said Seoul's policy of seeking reunification of the Korean peninsula by treating Pyongyang as an equal partner might have to be abandoned.
He did not elaborate but a senior New Korea Party official told Reuters the party chairman was stressing the need to brace South Korea for a possible collapse of the North.
In Beijing, China announced to its people for the first time on Wednesday that Hwang had entered the embassy of South Korea in the capital, and hinted that he had defected.
The official Xinhua news agency indicated that Hwang had sought refuge in Seoul's mission of his own free will.
Signs have emerged that North Korea might be ready to give up the fight to recover Hwang, possibly as a result of mediation by Beijing to end the Cold War crisis in its backyard.
The softer tone was first set when Pyongyang's Foreign Ministry said on Monday it would dismiss Hwang if he defected.

Japan's economic daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Wednesday that Kim Jong-u, head of North Korea's Overseas Economic Cooperation Committee, told a meeting with financial officials in China that Pyongyang had already dismissed Hwang.
Lee from Seoul's ruling party said Hwang must be granted political asylum in South Korea as he wished, but urged the South Korean media and citizens to be cautious and patient.
He said Pyongyang's woes would remain a headache for Seoul.
Apart from Hwang, many other North Koreans who had fled the North were awaiting defection to South Korea in China and elsewhere, he said without giving details.

Separately, an international consortium supervising the construction of nuclear reactors in North Korea was scheduled to ship seismology machinery and other instruments to the North despite Hwang's defection.
A South Korean Foreign Ministry official said the shipment by the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) would leave late on Wednesday.
But he said the defection crisis had delayed plans to send a 30-member site survey team into North Korea.

KEDO, a consortium led mostly by South Korea, Japan and the United States, is supervising the construction of two light water reactors being built in the North in exchange for Pyongyang freezing its suspected nuclear weapons programme.
Under the agreement signed in Geneva in October 1994, North Korea promised to dismantle its weapons-grade nuclear programme in return for several light-water reactors.
The deal was frozen when a Northern submarine infiltrated into South Korean waters in September, but a later apology from Pyongyang for the incident put the agreement back on track.
The two Koreas remain technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce and not a peace agreement.
